assessments.label: Adapting LLMs for Low-Resource Languages: Annotation, Retrieval, Translation, Code, and Fine-Tuning
assessments.rationale: The five papers share the broad theme of applying large language models to low-resource languages, but they address materially different tasks and methods: LLM-based annotation for NLI, sentiment, and news classification (W4392669965); zero-shot cross-lingual reranking for African languages (W4402671168); language-specific LoRA fine-tuning for machine translation on Asian languages (W4408280927); tokenizer adaptation for low-resource programming languages (W4412889388); and a case study of fine-tuning challenges on Azerbaijani covering data scarcity, morphology, and tokenization (W7165392193). No single research idea unites all members.
assessments.contrast: Unlike C3, which focuses on evaluating and benchmarking LLMs on specific low-resource language families (Indonesian, Austronesian, Mesoamerican) and on machine translation or benchmarking, C2 spans a wider variety of tasks (annotation, retrieval, translation, code generation, fine-tuning analysis) and language types (natural and programming). Unlike C6, which centers on multimodal models and continual learning strategies, C2 is limited to text-based LLM adaptation.

evidence.quote: To that extent, we seek to evaluate multilingual large language models (LLMs) for their potential to substitute or aid human-generated annotation efforts.We use LLMs to re-label publicly available datasets in LR languages for the tasks of natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and news classification.

To address this, we investigate how LLMs function as listwise rerankers in cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) systems with queries in English and passages in four African languages: Hausa, Somali, Swahili, and Yoruba.We analyze and compare the effectiveness of monolingual reranking using either query or document translations.

This study introduces Language-Specific Fine-Tuning with Low-rank adaptation (LSFTL), a method that enhances translation for low-resource languages by optimizing the multi-head attention and feed-forward networks of Transformer layers through low-rank matrix adaptation.

Large language models (LLMs), which are primarily trained on high-resource programming languages (HRPLs), tend to perform suboptimally for low-resource programming languages (LRPLs).This study investigates the impact of tokenizer adaptation methods on improving code generation for LRPLs.

We examine data scarcity, morphological complexity, tokenization problems and domain gaps that make model adaptation harder. We also review methods like data augmentation, cross-lingual pre-training and transfer learning and assess how well they work for Azerbaijani.

assessments.label: Evaluating and Building LLMs for Specific Low-Resource Language Families
assessments.rationale: All four papers concentrate on assessing or improving LLM performance for particular low-resource language families: Sinhala (W4402389783), Indonesian languages Balinese and Minangkabau (W4403364915), Austronesian Formosan languages (W4416034203), and Mesoamerican languages (W7162479607). They share a common research idea of evaluating LLMs on linguistically related, under-resourced languages and developing tailored benchmarks or models (NusaMT-7B, FormosanBench, data denoising and morphological generation for Mesoamerican languages).
assessments.contrast: C3 differs from C2 by focusing on evaluation and model building for coherent language families rather than a heterogeneous set of tasks across disparate languages. It also differs from C4, which targets domain-specific adaptations (folktales, dictionary building) rather than broad language-family evaluation, and from C5, which emphasizes humanities research opportunities and a single-language usability study.

evidence.quote: Although multilingual large language models have been available for some time, their performance on low-resourced languages such as Sinhala has been poor. We evaluated four recent LLMs on their performance directly in the Sinhala language, and by translation to and from English. We also evaluated their fine-tunability with a small amount of fine-tuning data.

Consequently, such LLMs suffer with alignment and have lagged behind State-of-The-Art (SoTA) neural machine translation (NMT) models in these settings. This paper introduces NusaMT-7B, an LLM-based machine translation model for low-resource Indonesian languages, starting with Balinese and Minangkabau.

Formosan languages-a subgroup of Austronesian languages spoken in Taiwan-are both linguistically rich and endangered, largely due to the sociolinguistic dominance of Mandarin.In this work, we introduce FORMOSANBENCH, the first benchmark for evaluating LLMs on low-resource Austronesian languages.

Six LRLs are used throughout this research: K'iche', Seri, Kaqchikel, Huave, Uspanteko, and Nahuatl. These languages are Mesoamerican languages spoken in Mexico and Guatemala. They are used as examples of possibilities for LRL research using LLMs; however, the findings are meant to be applicable to other LRLs as well. Noisy data refers to data that contains errors or inconsistencies.

assessments.label: Domain-Specific LLM Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages: Folklore and Lexicography
assessments.rationale: The two papers apply LLMs to distinct domain-specific problems for low-resource languages: one evaluates and adapts LLMs for representing folktales in Irish and Gaelic via classification tasks and continued pre-training (W4404389841), while the other proposes a conceptual framework for an electronic explanatory dictionary of Tajik integrating morphological analysis, lemmatization, and entry generation (W7197036362). The shared idea is domain-specific adaptation, but the tasks (folklore classification vs. dictionary construction) and languages (Celtic vs. Tajik) differ materially.
assessments.contrast: C4 contrasts with C2 and C3 by targeting specialized cultural and lexicographic domains rather than general NLP tasks or language-family benchmarking. It also differs from C5, which discusses broad humanities research opportunities and a Swahili usability study, whereas C4 presents concrete adaptation methods for two specific applications.

evidence.quote: Although a number of large language models (LLMs) claim to be able to represent low-resource langauges such as Irish and Gaelic, we present two classification tasks to explore how useful these representations are, and three adaptations to improve the performance of these models.

Based on a systematic survey of existing linguistic, statistical, and corpus resources, we propose a dictionary architecture that integrates modules for morphological analysis, lemmatization, semantic clustering, and dictionary entry generation using LLMs.

assessments.label: LLMs for Low-Resource Languages in Humanities Research and Swahili Usability
assessments.rationale: One paper provides a systematic review of LLM opportunities and challenges across linguistic variation, historical documentation, cultural expression, and literary analysis for low-resource languages in humanities (W4405173107), while the other reports a usability study of LLMs for Swahili with Tanzanian participants, highlighting data scarcity and architectural limitations (W7155356580). The common thread is low-resource languages and LLMs, but the scope (broad interdisciplinary review vs. single-language empirical usability) and contributions differ substantially.
assessments.contrast: C5 differs from C2–C4 by emphasizing humanities research perspectives and a user-centered evaluation rather than technical model adaptation, benchmarking, or domain-specific NLP tasks. It is also distinct from C6, which surveys multimodal models and continual learning techniques.

evidence.quote: This study systematically evaluates the applications of LLMs in low-resource language research, encompassing linguistic variation, historical documentation, cultural expressions, and literary analysis. By analyzing technical frameworks, current methodologies, and ethical considerations, this paper identifies key challenges such as data accessibility, model adaptability, and cultural sensitivity.

In this study, participants from Tanzanian Swahili-speaking communities evaluated the models' outputs through usability tests. Findings reveal that apart from architectural limitations, data scarcity drives the ineffectiveness of the models. Frequent distortions, mostly in Swahili than in French confirms the need for broader multilingual inclusion in LLM training.

assessments.label: Survey and Adaptation Methods for Low-Resource Languages in Multimodal and Text-Only LLMs
assessments.rationale: The cluster contains a survey of large multimodal models (LMMs) for low-resource languages (W4407385098) and multiple papers on adapting LLMs for low-resource languages using continual learning (W7123296616, W7123371404, W7155373379), contextual learning (W7154856337), and continued pre-training with benchmarking (W7165482954). The shared research idea is adapting large language models for low-resource languages, but the methods differ: some focus on multimodal models, others on text-only LLMs, and they employ distinct techniques (continual learning with POS-based code-switching, contextual learning with cross-lingual transfer, continued pre-training with data mixture strategies). The presence of a survey paper adds a meta-perspective. This heterogeneity in methods and model types (multimodal vs. text-only) makes the group mixed.
assessments.contrast: Unlike C11, which focuses specifically on Basque language adaptation using instruction tuning and multimodal training with synthetic data, C6 covers a broader set of low-resource languages (including African languages) and a wider range of adaptation methods (continual learning, contextual learning, continued pre-training, and a survey of multimodal models). C2 and C13 also focus on fine-tuning and LoRA for low-resource languages but are more specific to machine translation, annotation, or programming languages, whereas C6 includes both multimodal and text-only approaches across diverse language families.

evidence.quote: • Provides an open-source repository that includes implementation details, datasets, and benchmarks. In this survey, we systematically analyze techniques used to adapt large multimodal models (LMMs) for low-resource (LR) languages, examining approaches ranging from visual enhancement and data creation to cross-modal transfer and fusion strategies.

This work proposes to employ a continual learning strategy using parts-of-speech (POS)-based code-switching along with a replay adapter strategy to mitigate the identified gap of catastrophic forgetting while training SLM from LLM. Experiments conducted on vision language tasks such as visual question answering and language modelling task exhibits the success of the proposed architecture.

This paper proposes an efficient training strategy based on contextual learning, aimed at addressing the difficulties encountered by low-resource languages in zero-shot and few-shot learning scenarios.

Despite remarkable advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), African languagesremain critically underserved by the current training and adaptation pipeline. This thesisaddresses the fundamental bottlenecks in adapting LLMs for low-resource languagesthrough a unified two-stage investigation: benchmarking via Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT) and foundational adaptation via Continued Pre-Training (CPT).

assessments.label: Basque Language Adaptation of Large Language Models via Instruction Tuning and Multimodal Training
assessments.rationale: Both papers focus exclusively on adapting large language models for Basque, a low-resource language. W4417133178 systematically studies instruction adaptation pipelines using synthetic instructions and target language corpora, finding that instruction-tuned backbones outperform base models. W4416223637 develops a multimodal LLM for Basque using image-text datasets and shows that low ratios of Basque multimodal data suffice and a Basque-instructed backbone is not required. The shared task (Basque LLM adaptation), language (Basque), and use of synthetic or multimodal data create a coherent group.
assessments.contrast: C11 is tightly focused on a single low-resource language (Basque) and evaluates instruction tuning and multimodal training with synthetic data, whereas C6 covers multiple language families (including African languages) and diverse methods (continual learning, contextual learning, continued pre-training, and a multimodal survey). C3 benchmarks LLMs on various low-resource languages (Sinhala, Indonesian, Austronesian) but does not focus on adaptation methods for a specific language. C13 includes African languages and programming languages but lacks the systematic instruction tuning and multimodal focus on a single language seen in C11.

evidence.quote: Instructing language models with user intent requires large instruction datasets, which are only available for a limited set of languages. In this paper, we explore alternatives to conventional instruction adaptation pipelines in low-resource scenarios.

Our conclusions show that target language corpora are essential, with synthetic instructions yielding robust models, and, most importantly, that using as backbone an instruction-tuned model outperforms using a base non-instructed model. Scaling up to Llama 3.1 Instruct 70B as backbone, our model comes near frontier models of much larger sizes for Basque, without using any Basque instructions.

Current Multimodal Large Language Models exhibit very strong performance for several demanding tasks. While commercial MLLMs deliver acceptable performance in low-resource languages, comparable results remain unattained within the open science community. In this paper, we aim to develop a strong MLLM for a low-resource language, namely Basque.

We show that: i) low ratios of Basque multimodal data (around 20%) are already enough to obtain solid results on Basque benchmarks, and ii) contrary to expected, a Basque instructed backbone LLM is not required to obtain a strong MLLM in Basque. Our results pave the way to develop MLLMs for other low-resource languages by openly releasing our resources.

assessments.label: LLM Adaptation for Low-Resource African Languages and Programming Languages
assessments.rationale: The cluster contains two papers with distinct targets: W7115677253 focuses on adaptive and efficient LLMs for low-resource African languages using LoRA fine-tuning and synthetic data augmentation, while W7168097912 addresses reviving low-resource programming languages using LLMs. The only commonality is the use of LLMs for low-resource settings, but the domains (natural languages vs. programming languages) and adaptation goals differ significantly. There is no shared method, language family, or evaluation setting that unifies them.
assessments.contrast: C13 combines African natural languages and programming languages, whereas C6 includes African languages but focuses on multimodal models, continual learning, and continued pre-training for natural languages only. C2 and C13 both mention fine-tuning and LoRA for low-resource languages, but C2 is centered on machine translation, annotation, and tokenization for specific languages like Azerbaijani, while C13's programming language paper has no overlap with C2's natural language focus. The mismatch in C13 is between natural and programming language domains.

grade_decisions.reason: Too many single-paper clusters; lower the similarity threshold or merge.

Re-cluster by verifying paper contents rather than relying on title keywords. Merge duplicate records (W7123296616, W7123371404, W7155373379 are the same paper). Split C2 into coherent sub-clusters: one for annotation/reranking (W4392669965, W4402671168), one for translation fine-tuning (W4408280927, W4412889388), one for fine-tuning challenges (W7165392193). Merge C11 and C4 if they share domain adaptation methods. Treat title-only records (C9) as uncertain rather than a cluster. Ensure each cluster label reflects actual shared method/task/language family, not just broad topic.
